Preparation for the lesson
Students will make a paper Christmas cracker during this online lesson. Ask them to prepare the following materials before the lesson:
Two sheets of A4 paper for the cracker
One extra sheet of paper for practice
A pencil
A pen for writing a short message or joke
A small cardboard tube (e.g. half a kitchen roll tube) to help shape the cracker
A small paper surprise, such as a joke or a message
Students also need a clear, flat surface for folding paper.
Wordlist

paper crown — a paper hat that looks like a crown

Ex 1.2 Read the text. Which three things from Exercise 1.1 are inside a Christmas cracker?
A British Christmas Surprise
Imagine you're having Christmas dinner with a British family. There's a colourful paper tube next to your plate. It looks like a giant sweet, but you can't eat it. It's a Christmas cracker!
Here's the fun part. You hold one end, and someone else holds the other. You both pull. POP! The cracker opens with a bang.

What's inside? Usually, you'll find a paper crown, a joke and a small gift, such as a tiny small toy. First, you look inside. Then people put on their crowns and read the jokes aloud. The jokes are often very silly. Here's one:
“What do you call a snowman in summer?”
“A puddle!”
You can make your own paper cracker, too. Fold the paper, put a little surprise inside and give it to a friend. Your paper cracker won't make a bang, but it's still a fun Christmas present.
Suggested answer
A. A paper crown
B. A small toy
C. A joke

We use imperatives to tell someone what to do.

Imperatives

Start with the base form of a verb. We don't usually need you.

Fold the paper.

Hold the paper.

Sequencing words

We use sequencing words to show the order of actions.

First, — the beginning

Next, — the next step

Then, — another step

Finally, — the last step

Example

First, take the paper.

Next, fold it in half.

Then, open it.

Finally, turn it over.

parts.title: Look at the pictures and make your own paper Christmas cracker
parts.html:
Work with a partner or your teacher:

  • Look at the next picture
  • Say what to do
  • Follow the instruction and check your paper
  • Take turns giving instructions
  • Use first, next, then and finally

What you need

  • Two sheets of A4 paper
  • A pencil
  • A cardboard tube (to help shape the cracker)
  • A small paper surprise, such as a joke or a message

Useful phrases

Giving instructions
First, take…
Next, fold…
Then, turn it over.
Hold this side.
Finally, put … inside.

Checking
Like this?
Is this right?
What's next?

Sample answer

Student A: First, take a sheet of paper.
Student B: OK. What's next?
Student A: Next, fold this side.
Student B: Like this?
Student A: Yes, that's right! Now turn it over.
Student B: OK. Then, fold it again?
Student A: Yes! Great!

Students continue following the picture guide.

Student B: Finally, open the cracker and put your surprise inside.
Student A: Done! It looks great!

The Cracker That Didn't Pop!

It's the afternoon of the school Christmas party. Lily and Sam are getting their paper Christmas crackers ready.

‘I think mine's ready,’ says Lily. ‘How's yours?’

‘Not great,’ says Sam. ‘I can't fold this part.’

‘Here, hold the paper like this,’ Lily says. ‘Now fold this side.’

‘Oh, I see. Thanks!’

Lily puts a paper crown and a silly joke inside her cracker. Sam writes a note and puts it in his. The note says: ‘You can choose the first song at our Christmas party!’

A little later, Ben comes into the classroom.

‘Wow, Christmas crackers!’ he says. ‘Can I pull one? I love that loud POP!’

‘Our crackers don't pop,’ Lily explains. ‘We made them ourselves. Just open one.’

Sam gives Ben his cracker. Ben opens it and reads the note.

‘Really? I can choose the first song? That's even better than a pop!’ he laughs. ‘Can we make more for our friends?’

‘Great idea!’ says Lily.
